title: Nigerian Pidgin
motto: The most expressive, energetic lingua franca across West Africa!
description: Learn the vibrant language spoken by over 75 million people across Nigeria, West Africa, and global Afrobeat culture — structured with the NERDC 4-Tier Oracy, Grammar, and Literature framework.

proverbOfDay.proverb: Monkey dey work, baboon dey chop.
proverbOfDay.translation: One person toils while another unjustly enjoys the fruit of the labor.
proverbOfDay.context: The master proverb of Nigerian civic and commercial discourse, addressing unfair compensation, uncredited teamwork, and the struggle for equity.

cultureTips.title: The Sacred Greeting: 'How You Dey?' & Tone Variations
cultureTips.description: When meeting anyone in Nigeria, a cheerful 'How you dey?' or 'How far?' breaks all social friction. The reply can vary from 'I dey fine' (standard), to 'We dey push am' (humble resilience), or 'I dey kampe' (unshakeable energy).

cultureTips.title: The Danfo Transit Etiquette & 'Owa o!'
cultureTips.description: In the famous yellow Danfo buses across Lagos, passengers must always alert the conductor before their stop by loudly calling 'Owa o!' (meaning 'Someone is alighting here!'). Always carry 'change' (small denomination notes) to avoid conductor disputes.

cultureTips.title: Food Hospitality: The Compulsory 'Come and Chop!'
cultureTips.description: Whenever you are eating in the presence of colleagues, guests, or neighbors, it is cultural etiquette to warmly invite them: 'Come and chop!' A polite refusal is simply: 'Thank you, I dey alright' or 'Enjoy your food.'

cultureTips.title: The Magic Softener: 'Abeg'
cultureTips.description: 'Abeg' literally translates to 'I beg you' (Please). Placing 'Abeg' at the beginning or end of a question instantly diffuses tension, conveys mutual respect, and turns any hard negotiation into a warm transaction.

cultureTips.title: The Art of Market Haggling: 'How Much Last?'
cultureTips.description: In open-air markets (like Balogun, Ariaria, or Bodija), the quoted initial price is never final. The buyer begins by asking 'How much last, my sister?' Building rapport, laughing together, and calling the seller 'Customer' or 'Oga/Madam' guarantees the best price.

cultureTips.title: Respect for Elders: 'Bros', 'Uncle', and 'Ma'
cultureTips.description: Never call an elder or senior acquaintance by their bare first name in NPE. Prefixing with 'Bros' (for older peers), 'Uncle/Aunty' (for generationally older contacts), or 'Sir/Ma' reflects the deep communal respect foundational to Nigerian culture.

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Dental Fricative Shift & Initial H Dropping
lessons.description: Master standard consonant sound substitutions (thing -> ting, them -> dem) and the dropping of initial 'h' (house -> ouse).

questions.prompt: In Nigerian Pidgin phonology, how is the English voiceless dental fricative 'th' in 'thing' pronounced?
options: It remains identical to British English 'thing'
questions.explanation: Nigerian Pidgin (West Africa) systematically replaces the voiceless dental fricative /θ/ with the alveolar plosive /t/ (thing -> ting, thank -> tank, three -> tree).

questions.prompt: How does the voiced 'th' in 'them' or 'they' sound in standard Nigerian Pidgin?
questions.explanation: The voiced dental fricative /ð/ systematically becomes /d/, producing 'dem' (them/they), 'dat' (that), and 'dis' (this).

questions.prompt: What happens to the initial 'h' sound in words like 'house' or 'hospital' in everyday Pidgin speech?
options: The /h/ is intensified into a harsh guttural sound
An extra 'k' is added before the /h/
It is always pronounced with British RP precision
questions.explanation: NPE phonotactics frequently drops initial voiceless glottal fricatives /h/, yielding 'ouse' for house, 'ospital' for hospital, and 'ungry' for hungry.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: 'I want go back to my _____ (house).'
questions.sentence: I want go back to my ___ (house).
questions.explanation: With the initial /h/ dropped, 'house' is rendered as 'ouse'.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: 'No worry yourself, na small _____ (thing) dey happen.'
questions.sentence: No worry yourself, na small ___ (thing) dey happen.
questions.explanation: 'Thing' becomes 'ting' through dental fricative replacement /θ/ -> /t/.

questions.prompt: How is the English word 'three' pronounced in Pidgin when counting items?
questions.explanation: 'Three' shifts phonetically to 'tree' (/θriː/ -> /tri/). E.g. 'Give me tree bottle of water.'

questions.prompt: How does the English word 'think' appear in spoken Nigerian Pidgin?
questions.explanation: 'Think' becomes 'tink' (e.g. 'Wetin you tink say make we do?').

questions.prompt: How is 'thank you' typically rendered in natural Pidgin interaction?
questions.explanation: Voiceless /θ/ becomes /t/ ('tank you'), often doubled with 'well-well' for gratitude.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: 'Give _____ (them) their books.'
questions.sentence: Give ___ (them) their books.
questions.explanation: The object pronoun 'them' is rendered as 'dem'.

questions.prompt: In the word 'thief', how is the initial sound transformed in Pidgin?
questions.explanation: 'Thief' is pronounced and written as 'tief' (/tiːf/).

questions.prompt: Which of the following demonstrates initial /h/ dropping in the word 'heart'?
questions.explanation: Initial /h/ dropping renders 'heart' as 'art'.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: 'I dey feel heavy _____ (hunger) for belly.'
questions.sentence: I dey feel heavy ___ (hunger) for belly.
questions.explanation: 'Hunger/hungry' drops initial /h/, frequently expressed as 'ungry dey catch me'.

questions.prompt: How is 'that' pronounced and spelled in standard Nigerian Pidgin (West Africa)?
questions.explanation: 'That' becomes 'dat' (e.g. 'Dat book wey dey table').

questions.prompt: How is 'this' rendered in standard Nigerian Pidgin (West Africa)?
questions.explanation: 'This' becomes 'dis' (e.g. 'Dis lesson sweet well-well').

questions.prompt: What does the high-frequency verb 'chop' mean in Nigerian Pidgin?

questions.explanation: 'Una' (derived from Igbo 'ụnụ') is the universal second person plural pronoun in Nigerian Pidgin.

questions.prompt: What pronoun is used for the 3rd person singular subject ('he' or 'she') in Nigerian Pidgin?

A past tense suffix like English '-ed'

Future marker meaning 'I will be fine'

questions.explanation: When followed by an adjective or state, 'dey' functions as a stative copula denoting state or condition.

options: Dynamic auxiliary marking continuous/progressive action ('I am reading the Bible')
questions.correctAnswer: Dynamic auxiliary marking continuous/progressive action ('I am reading the Bible')
questions.explanation: When placed before an active verb, 'dey' (or 'de' in standard literary orthography) marks ongoing continuous aspect.

questions.prompt: How is the plural form of nouns created in standard Nigerian Pidgin?
options: By placing 'dem' immediately after the noun ('book dem', 'boy dem')
By adding an '-s' or '-es' suffix like English
By adding 'many' before every noun without exception
questions.correctAnswer: By placing 'dem' immediately after the noun ('book dem', 'boy dem')
questions.explanation: Nigerian Pidgin does not use plural inflections like '-s'. Instead, it uses the post-nominal marker 'dem' (e.g. 'pikin dem' = children).

questions.prompt: In standard Nigerian Pidgin, how are collective groups or communities referred to when describing people?
questions.explanation: In standard Nigerian Pidgin, collective categories and community groups are formed using 'people' (e.g. 'our people', 'village people') or 'dem' (e.g. 'teacher dem').

questions.prompt: What does reduplication like 'fine-fine' or 'big-big' express in Nigerian Pidgin?
options: Plurality, intensity, or variety across items ('all kinds of beautiful / big things')
questions.correctAnswer: Plurality, intensity, or variety across items ('all kinds of beautiful / big things')
questions.explanation: Reduplication functions distributively and intensively: 'fine-fine cloth' = various lovely clothes.

questions.sentence: Call all the teacher ___ (plural marker) make they come.
questions.explanation: 'Teacher dem' = the teachers.

questions.prompt: What does 'The pikin dem dey play ball' mean?

questions.prompt: If someone says 'E pack plenty sweet-sweet mango', what does 'sweet-sweet' imply?

The mangoes had sugar artificially added to them

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: 'The student _____ (plural) don pass their exam.'

questions.prompt: Can a numeral make the plural explicit without 'dem', as in 'tree book'?

No, 'dem' is strictly forbidden with numbers
No, you must always add an English '-s'
questions.correctAnswer: Yes, when a cardinal number precedes the noun, 'dem' is optional ('tree book' or 'the tree book dem')
questions.explanation: Numerals alone ('tree book') can carry plurality, but 'dem' may be added for definite specificity ('the tree book dem').

questions.prompt: What does 'quick-quick' mean in 'Make we go quick-quick'?

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Directional Serial Verbs (Take... Come/Go)
lessons.description: Master multi-verb serial sequences expressing transfer and movement: Take... Come ('bring'), Carry... Go ('take away'), and Run... Enter ('run into').

questions.prompt: What is a Serial Verb Construction (SVC) in Nigerian Pidgin?
options: Two or more verbs chained together in a single clause under one subject without conjunctions
A sentence with multiple commas and exclamation marks
A list of irregular Latin verbs
A verb followed by five adverbs
questions.correctAnswer: Two or more verbs chained together in a single clause under one subject without conjunctions
questions.explanation: Inherited from West African languages (Niger-Congo substrate), SVCs combine verbs like 'take', 'come', 'go', and 'give' into a single conceptual predicate.

questions.prompt: How do you say 'Bring that book here' using an SVC with 'take' and 'come'?
options: 'Take dat book come' or 'Take dat book come give me'
questions.correctAnswer: 'Take dat book come' or 'Take dat book come give me'
questions.explanation: 'Take [object] come' is the classic SVC structure replacing the single English verb 'bring'.

questions.prompt: What does 'Carry am go' mean in everyday Pidgin?
options: 'Take it away' / 'Remove it to another location'
questions.correctAnswer: 'Take it away' / 'Remove it to another location'
questions.explanation: 'Carry [object] go' denotes movement away from the speaker ('take away').

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: '_____ (Take) the water come make I drink.'
questions.sentence: ___ (Take) the water come make I drink.
questions.explanation: 'Take [item] come' introduces the object in a directional SVC.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: 'The boy run _____ (enter) inside the room.'
questions.sentence: The boy run ___ (enter) inside the room.
questions.explanation: 'Run enter' chains the manner of motion ('run') with entry ('enter').

questions.correctAnswer: 'See how this video take make the story about Jesus life dey real to us'
questions.explanation: Standard media Pidgin: 'See how this sweet video take make the story about Jesus Christ life dey real to us' ('take make' = instrumental causation).

questions.prompt: What does the SVC 'E fly pass over the fence' signify?
options: It flew completely over the fence
questions.correctAnswer: It flew completely over the fence
questions.explanation: 'Fly pass' combines manner ('fly') with spatial traversal ('pass').

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: 'Pack all these plate _____ (go) kitchen.'
questions.sentence: Pack all these plate ___ (go) kitchen.
questions.explanation: 'Pack [items] go [place]' combines collecting with directional movement.

questions.prompt: In the sentence 'E climb tree fall down', how many verbs form the serial event?
questions.explanation: A classic narrative SVC depicting climbing followed immediately by falling.

questions.prompt: How do you translate 'He escaped by running into the bush'?
questions.explanation: 'Run enter' is the standard directional serial compound.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: 'Carry the heavy load _____ (come) house.'

questions.explanation: 'Carry [object] come' indicates transporting something toward the speaker.

questions.prompt: Can you put the English conjunction 'and' between verbs in an authentic SVC?
options: No, true serial verbs occur without 'and' ('Take am come', not 'Take am and come')
Yes, 'and' must always be inserted between every word
Only when speaking to older people
questions.correctAnswer: No, true serial verbs occur without 'and' ('Take am come', not 'Take am and come')

questions.explanation: 'Make you do am' is a causative SVC sequence.
